subject: Nvidia stops shipping AI servers to Southeast Asia
bodyMarkdown:
Washington published a new chip rule nine days ago, and overnight we learned what it does in practice. Nvidia has stopped AI servers from reaching four countries that were supposed to be the comfortable middle ground of the global AI build out, and that lands on you this morning whether you hold tech funds or you are waiting on a Canadian data centre.

## What Nvidia stopped

The Financial Times reported overnight that Nvidia told its manufacturing partners to halt AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, citing three people with knowledge of the matter. Dell and Supermicro, the companies that actually assemble and ship most of those racks, told buyers in those countries their orders would not be released. Nvidia has not issued a statement, and nobody in the reporting will say whether the freeze runs for days or quarters. The same reporting says cloud operators in the region now have 90 days to show their services do not reach restricted customers. I read a pause with no stated end date as a policy rather than a hiccup. Malaysia and Indonesia have the most at stake, since both have been collecting billions in announced AI site investment on the promise that the chips would show up.

## The rule behind it

The trigger is an interim final rule from the US Bureau of Industry and Security, titled Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors, released on November 16 and effective when it hit the Federal Register on November 19. Akin Gump's client alert on the rule lays out the mechanism. A new section 744.24 requires a licence when the exporter knows the chips are headed to a data centre, anywhere on earth, that supplies more than 12 million aggregate **total processing performance** (Washington's unit for how much computing a pile of chips can do) to companies headquartered in China or other restricted countries. The rule also formally rescinds the Biden era AI Diffusion Rule and adds country level licensing for five destinations: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Comments close January 19. Control has moved from where a chip physically sits to who is allowed to log into it.

## What it means for your money and for Canada

Nvidia reported its October quarter on November 17: revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, with $107.6 billion of that from data centres. Guidance for the current quarter is $130 billion, and the company said that figure assumes no data centre compute revenue from China at all. The China hole is already in the forecast. The open question is how much other business gets caught in the fight over diversion, and CNBC reported on Wednesday that an unusual volume of Nvidia GPUs has come up for resale since the rule landed, with sellers hunting for buyers. Canada sits outside the five flagged destinations, which quietly improves the case for building here. Ottawa's Budget 2026, released November 5, pledges help securing 500 megawatts of domestically controlled compute and counts more than 200 data centre projects in the pipeline, including Bell's planned 1.2 gigawatt hub in Saskatchewan.

## The takeaway

Watch whether the Southeast Asia freeze lifts within a couple of weeks, because a pause that runs into late December stops being a compliance delay and starts being lost revenue for Dell, Supermicro and the sites waiting on racks. If you hold a tech heavy fund, the exposure worth checking is the reach of the diversion crackdown into third countries, since Nvidia has already written China down to zero in its own guidance. For Canadian projects, ask who an operator is allowed to rent its compute to, because that is now an export control question as much as a power question. The comment period closes January 19, and that is when the industry pushback shows up on the public record.
